name: THE FRIED OFF INTO THE SUNSET BURGER (comes with a fried egg)

recipe.history:
The fried egg has been a human food for as long as we have kept domesticated chickens — a practice that likely began in Southeast Asia and the Indian subcontinent somewhere between seven and ten thousand years ago. The egg fried over open heat is perhaps the most universal preparation in the global culinary repertoire, appearing in the cuisines of virtually every culture that keeps poultry. But the specific aesthetic of a fried egg with a bright, deeply orange-yolked sunny-side-up presentation — the one that evokes a sunset, with its vivid disc of yolk surrounded by the opaque white — is a product of the hen's diet and breed as much as of cooking technique. The deep orange, almost amber yolks associated with pasture-raised or free-range hens come from the carotenoid pigments xanthophyll and beta-carotene, absorbed from grass, insects, marigold petals, and other forage unavailable to battery hens eating only grain. The French, who have long treated the egg as a subject worthy of serious culinary attention, developed the concept of the oeuf sur le plat — the egg fried in butter in a small pan or gratin dish, served with the yolk trembling and intact — as a dish in its own right, not merely a component. Spanish huevos fritos, fried in a deep pool of olive oil until the edges lacework and the white puffs and blisters, represent another tradition of equal sophistication. Across these traditions, the fried egg is treated with a reverence it rarely receives in American short-order cooking.

The egg on a burger is an American invention that draws from multiple culinary traditions simultaneously. The "Loco Moco," a Hawaiian dish of rice, burger patty, and fried egg covered in brown gravy, popularized the burger-plus-egg combination on the mainland during the mid-twentieth century, and by the 1980s and 1990s the "egg burger" had become a menu staple at upscale diners and brunch-forward restaurants across the country. The appeal is elemental: the fat of the yolk is the richest, most voluptuous condiment imaginable — it coats, lubricates, and enriches every element it touches. A runny yolk on a burger patty is functionally a sauce, one that was manufactured by a chicken and requires only butter and a hot pan to release. The visual drama of the yolk — that sunset orange globe, set against the white of the cooked albumen — gives the burger a beauty that no composed sauce can quite replicate. The yolk breaks on the first bite and flows into every layer, binding the whole construction together in a way that is as functional as it is magnificent.

I associate fried eggs on burgers with a specific diner in the Catskills where I used to stop on long drives upstate. The place had a counter with twelve stools and a cook who had been working the same flat-top griddle for what appeared to be several decades. He would crack an egg onto a corner of the griddle where a small pool of butter sat, season it with salt and pepper while the white was still translucent, and slide the whole thing — yolk still raw, white barely set at the edges — onto a patty he had just pulled off the grill. The residual heat from the patty would finish the white during the thirty seconds it took to assemble the burger, leaving the yolk just warm enough to be liquid but not cooked. I have never seen anyone else time it that precisely, and I have been trying to replicate it ever since. The key is that the egg should be a passenger — it should complete the burger, not dominate it. The yolk is the sunset. Everything else is the landscape it illuminates.

Cooking the burger patty to medium rare — 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) — is doubly important on a burger that will carry a fried egg with a runny yolk. The philosophy is one of coherence: if the yolk is liquid and the beef is dry, the yolk becomes merely a sauce applied to a puck, like ketchup or mustard. But if the yolk is liquid and the beef is also at its juiciest — pink, yielding, fat still in solution — then the two liquids merge in the mouth into something richer and more complex than either alone. The fried egg atop a medium-rare patty is not an indulgence. It is a completion — the final saturate color added to a sunset that was already beautiful. A well-done patty with a runny egg is a contradiction; a medium-rare patty with a runny egg is a philosophy made edible.
ingredients: 2 large eggs (1 for dough, 1 beaten for egg wash)
4 large pasture-raised eggs (for deeply orange, sunset-colored yolks)
Kosher salt and freshly cracked black pepper, to season
2 tbsp sun-dried tomato paste or finely minced sun-dried tomatoes in oil
4 strips thick-cut bacon, cooked until crisp
1 small red onion, thinly sliced into rings
instructions: 1. Make the brioche buns: Bloom the yeast with warm water and 1 tablespoon of sugar for 5 minutes. Add flour, remaining sugar, salt, 1 egg, warm milk, and softened butter. Knead in a stand mixer with the dough hook 8 to 10 minutes until smooth. Rise in an oiled bowl for 1 to 1 1/2 hours until doubled. Shape into 4 tight rounds, proof on a parchment-lined baking sheet 45 minutes. Brush with beaten egg, bake at 375°F (190°C) 15 to 18 minutes until golden. Cool on a rack.

2. Cook the bacon: Lay the bacon strips in a cold skillet and cook over medium heat, turning once, until crisp and deeply browned, 8 to 10 minutes total. Transfer to a paper-towel-lined plate. Reserve the bacon fat in the pan.

3. Make the smoky tomato aioli: Whisk together the mayonnaise, sun-dried tomato paste, smoked paprika, grated garlic, lemon juice, and salt in a small bowl until smooth and evenly orange-red in color. Taste and adjust seasoning. Refrigerate until assembly.

4. Form the burger patties: Divide the ground beef into 4 equal portions (8 oz / 227g each). Gently shape into patties approximately 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick. Press a shallow dimple into the center of each. Season both sides generously with salt and pepper immediately before cooking.

5. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking hot. Cook the patties 3 to 4 minutes on the first side without moving, building a deep, dark crust. Flip once. Immediately place one slice of cheddar on each patty. Cover and cook 2 to 3 more minutes until the internal temperature reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) and the cheese is melted. Transfer the patties to a wire rack and rest 3 minutes.

6. Fry the eggs: While the patties rest, return the skillet (or use a separate nonstick pan) to medium heat. Add the butter and let it foam and subside. Crack each egg carefully into the pan, keeping the yolks intact. Season the whites immediately with salt and pepper. Cook over medium heat, tilting the pan occasionally to baste the whites with the hot butter, until the whites are just set and fully opaque but the yolks are still completely liquid and glossy — approximately 2 to 3 minutes. The yolk should be a deep, vivid orange, like the low sun on the horizon. Do not flip; this is a sunny-side-up egg.
7. While the eggs cook, split the brioche buns and toast cut-side down in a dry skillet or on the griddle for 60 to 90 seconds until lightly golden.

8. Assemble: Spread the smoky tomato aioli generously on both bun halves. On the bottom bun, place a leaf of butter lettuce, then 2 slices of heirloom tomato, then the red onion rings. Place the cheddar-topped patty over the onions. Lay the crispy bacon strip across the patty. Using a thin spatula, gently slide one fried egg directly on top of the bacon, yolk facing up. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt. Cap with the top bun very gently — do not press down. Serve immediately, with hot sauce on the side if desired. The yolk will break on the first bite.
